**The survey rests on 5,653 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center and the Office of Scientific and Technical Information**, of which 3,172, being 56.1 percent, are report primaries by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **638 of the 5,556 dated records, being 11.5 percent, were published between 1946 and 1961**, the life of the programme, and 2,086, being 37.5 percent, date from 2015 or later. The median publication year is 1999, and the records fall into 13 clusters.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is read from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is a NASA Technical Reports Server citation, a record of the Office of Scientific and Technical Information, or a digital object identifier under the 10.2172 prefix, which Crossref registers for the Department of Energy reports that office holds, or under the 10.21236 prefix, which it registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **One Department of Energy report is reachable both as an office record and as a 10.2172 identifier**, and the survey cites each such report once. Of the 3,172 report primaries, 2,646 are Department of Energy reports, 436 are NASA reports and 90 are Defense Technical Information Center reports.

**The rule does not reach the journal papers that the programme's own engineers published**, so 56.1 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand. The documents that carry the argument are the progress reports and comprehensive technical reports named above, and every one of them is a report primary by this rule.

### Thin Subjects

**Six subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the reactor-to-crew separation and the divided shield | divided shield, unit shield, shadow shield, separation distance, crew compartment, crew shield | 16 |
| air activation in a direct-cycle engine | argon-41, nitrogen-16, air activation, activation of air, activated air | 12 |
| core heat-up and melting after loss of cooling | meltdown, melt-down, core melt, melting, heat-up | 7 |
| decay heat in a reactor that moves | decay heat, afterheat or decay heating, together with aircraft, mobile, transportable, ship, marine, naval, space, rocket, propulsion, microreactor or heat pipe | 10 |
| the dose to a crew from a reactor carried with it | crew, aircrew, personnel or pilot within eighty characters of reactor, nuclear powered or nuclear aircraft | 2 |
| shield mass against reactor power | shield weight, shield mass or shield thickness within sixty characters of power, megawatt or MW | 2 |

**The separation optimum is the clearest case of a subject answered elsewhere.** 13 of the 16 records concern the shadow shield, which covers only the solid angle the crew occupies, and the three most recent, all from 2022, are for reactors in space. No title names the separation between a reactor and a crew inside one fuselage as the quantity to be optimised. **Air activation is thin in a different way**, since its records concern stack releases, research reactors, water coolants and measurement technique, and none concerns air drawn through a core to propel an aircraft, which is the direct cycle's defining property.

**Decay heat is not a thin subject, but decay heat in a reactor that moves is.** The decay heat cluster holds 291 records naming it, and 10 of all the survey's records join it to a mobile, marine, space or propulsion reactor. **That a shield's thickness grows with the logarithm of reactor power is almost never published as a finding**, because it follows from the exponential attenuation law in one line, so the article's claim stands on the relation rather than on a literature.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is the nuclear aircraft, its reactor, its shield, the descendants of each, and what replaced the aircraft's mission. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Shielding also names the self-shielding of resonance cross sections, electromagnetic and acoustic shielding, debris shields and the thermal radiation shields of cryostats and Stirling engines. Radiation also names thermal and solar radiation, a reactor is also a chemical, electrical or plasma vessel, and a microreactor is also a device for flow chemistry. Pluto is also the name of a research reactor at Harwell, the acronym of the programme is also that of atrial natriuretic peptide, and the name of its predecessor project, NEPA, is also that of the National Environmental Policy Act. Lithium hydride is also a chemical reagent, a scattered-radiation measurement is also a radiograph, and the attenuation of gamma rays also measures soil, wood, grain and ore. Fusion devices, particle accelerators, medical radiology, aircraft striking a reactor and nuclear aircraft carriers are excluded as other subjects. Correction, retraction and withdrawal notices, abstracts of other papers and the front and back matter of books are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. Book reviews, reference, encyclopedia and dictionary entries other than authored articles of more than two pages, unsigned news items, and a second deposit of a document already held, such as a preprint of a kept article or a repository copy of a kept report, are not admitted either, because the first three are not research works and the last would count one work twice.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Decay heat measurement for power reactors, aircrew exposure to cosmic radiation, shielding materials developed for medical and industrial radiation, and the high-temperature gas-cooled power reactor line each share a method or a quantity with this subject, so each is kept and a reader may weigh it accordingly. The 1948 index to the Lexington Project reports is cited in the body as evidence of how the study was organised, and since an index is not a research work it is listed under Reference and not counted in the survey. The records that sit furthest from the aircraft among those the body cites, on semiconductor radiation effects, accelerator shielding and ship propulsion, are kept because the passages citing them use them as neighbouring science.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** No sample measures it, and what remains is whatever a reader of titles alone could misjudge.

## Epistemic State

Established historical fact includes the start of Project NEPA on 28 May 1946 under the Army Air Forces, its replacement by the joint AEC and Air Force ANP programme in May 1951, the assignment of the direct air cycle to General Electric and the indirect cycle to Pratt and Whitney, the MX-1589 modification of two B-36 airframes, the tornado damage to 51-5712 at Carswell on 1 September 1952, its rebuilding as the NB-36H, its carriage of the one megawatt Aircraft Shield Test Reactor, its 47 flights and 215 hours between 17 September 1955 and March 1957 with the reactor operated for 89 of those hours, the operation of the Aircraft Reactor Experiment at Oak Ridge in 1954 as the first molten salt reactor, the ground testing of a direct-cycle nuclear turbojet in the HTRE series, and the cancellation of the X-6 work at Convair in 1953, and the cancellation of the programme in March 1961 without the X-6 being built.

Established engineering analysis includes every relation in the sizing sections. The exponential attenuation law with buildup, the logarithmic dependence of shield thickness on power and on dose limit, the separation optimum, the Way-Wigner decay heat correlation, the turbojet thrust and heat addition relations, and the heat exchanger effectiveness relation are standard results.

**Derived here and not taken from a source** are the hundred megawatt thermal power estimate for a B-36-class cruise, the 0.44 kilogram uranium consumption over a hundred hours, the gamma source strength and the ten gray per second unshielded dose rate at ten metres, the attenuation requirement of $7.1 \times 10^{7}$ that follows from a fifty millisievert mission limit, the 25.7 centimetre lead thickness and the 222 centimetre lithium hydride thickness, the 8.7 centimetre thickness increment for a thousandfold power increase, the 10.1 metre separation optimum, the 41 tonne gamma shield mass with a 66 tonne upper bound including neutrons and their ratios to gross weight and payload, the 100 megawatt per cubic metre core power density, the 1211 kelvin indirect-cycle reactor outlet requirement, the 23 minute adiabatic melt time, and the decay heat figures. These follow by arithmetic from published dimensions and standard physical constants and can be reproduced or refuted by any reader with them.

Inference includes the central claim that the shield mass rather than any other difficulty was the binding constraint, and the subsidiary claim that the logarithmic dependence made the programme insensitive to relaxing the crew dose limit. Both are consistent with the record and with the fact that shield optimization was a named research subject throughout the programme, but neither is a statement the primary reports make in those terms.

Weakly supported are the representative values. The lift-to-drag ratio of eighteen, the cruise speed of 200 metres per second, the overall propulsive efficiency of 0.20, the shadow shield area of 14.1 square metres, the fuselage structural mass of 400 kilograms per metre, the fifty millisievert mission dose allowance from which the attenuation requirement follows, the four percent gamma energy fraction, the mean photon energy of one megaelectronvolt, the lithium hydride removal cross-section, the buildup factor of ten, the six square metre crew shield area used in the comparison with the NB-36H, and the five tonne core mass used in the melt-time estimate are all plausible figures for the class rather than values taken from the design. The shield mass estimate should be read as establishing an order of magnitude and a ratio, not a design number. The ratio is more trustworthy than the absolute value, and the qualitative conclusion that shielding consumes a payload-sized fraction of a B-36 is robust to any reasonable choice of inputs.

Contested or unresolved in the sources consulted is the total programme cost, given as about one billion dollars by the [Comptroller General][ref_gao_anp_1963] and seven billion in the [X-6 entry][ref_convair_x6], a discrepancy most plausibly explained by inflation adjustment but not stated as such by either source. NEPA's 1947 funding of ten million dollars rests on a single secondary account. The crew shield mass is given as eleven tons in the [NB-36H entry][ref_nb36h] and twelve in the [X-6 entry][ref_convair_x6], neither saying whether short or metric tons are meant, and read as short tons the computed 11.2 and 12.7 tonnes would both lie above the reported range rather than bracket it. The window thickness is given as six inches in one account and ten to twelve in another, and the scrapping of the NB-36H is placed at Fort Worth in 1958 in one account and at Carswell in 1957 in another. None of these are load-bearing for the argument, and all are stated here as reported rather than resolved.

A note on temporal position. This article carries an editorial date of 2025-10-12 and is written from current knowledge, including contemporary literature published well after that date.

## Conclusion

The Convair X-6 was never built, and what it would have had to carry can be computed in a page.

A B-36 at cruise needs about a hundred megawatts of thermal power, and a reactor supplying it consumes less than half a kilogram of uranium in a hundred hours against 837 tonnes of kerosene for the same energy. That factor of nearly two million is the entire attraction. Unshielded at ten metres that reactor delivers about ten grays per second, when about five grays is a median lethal dose, so one second of exposure would kill the crew. Holding them to fifty millisieverts over a hundred-hour flight demands an attenuation of seven times ten to the seventh, or twenty-six centimetres of lead, and the geometry that minimizes the total mass puts the reactor about ten metres from the crew, which a B-36 fuselage accommodates easily. The gamma shield that results weighs about 41 tonnes, twenty-two percent of the aircraft and slightly more than the whole of its bomb load, and the neutron layer takes the upper bound to about 66 tonnes. **A nuclear bomber buys unlimited range by surrendering the payload that made the range worth having.**

The exponential that makes shielding work also makes it stubborn. Shield thickness depends on the logarithm of reactor power, so a thousandfold increase in power costs under nine centimetres of lead. The shield is therefore a fixed overhead and not a proportional cost, and small nuclear aircraft are not merely difficult but excluded. The same logarithm means that accepting ten times the crew dose saves about two and a half percent of the aircraft. The programme could not have been rescued by being braver.

One aircraft flew and it was not the X-6. The NB-36H carried a one megawatt reactor 47 times to measure what shielding does, and it established that the shielding worked, for a source a hundred times smaller than the one that would have propelled it. A direct-cycle nuclear turbojet ran on a test stand in Idaho and produced thrust from fission. The programme reached that point and was cancelled in 1961, not because the shield defeated it but because ballistic missiles and aerial refuelling had made an indefinitely loitering bomber a solution without a problem.

What survives is a reactor. The Aircraft Reactor Experiment ran at Oak Ridge in 1954 as the world's first molten salt reactor, built for high temperature and high power density, which a molten salt core gives at low pressure. An aircraft wants that combination and, as it turns out, so does a good deal else. Seventy years later that concept is under commercial development while the aircraft it was invented for remains unbuilt. An effort that produces no aircraft and one durable reactor technology has not failed in any sense worth the word, and the fact that it is remembered as a failure is a defect in how such work is scored, not in what this one did.

The next article takes the [Lockheed X-7][ref_list_of_x_planes], a ramjet test vehicle that was launched rather than flown, and asks what changes when the aircraft is expendable.
